title: How to Automate Business Payments Solutions in UAE
summary: Practical playbook for UAE finance teams to automate payments, reduce FX surprises, and tighten upstream controls, with AP, approvals, and reconciliation.
body_text: According to recent industry research, more than 80% of finance leaders now consider accounts payable automation a core part of their digital transformation agenda. That shift says less about technology maturity and more about pressure: pressure to explain cash movement with confidence, defend variances, and close books without firefighting. For many finance teams in the UAE, the weakest point in the payments process is not intent, but timing and visibility. An invoice may be approved on paper, yet the final cost only becomes clear after the payment is executed. FX differences surface days later. Approvals are rushed because suppliers are waiting, and month-end conversations turn into justification exercises rather than analysis. This is why business payments automation has moved up the finance priority list. For organisations making frequent or high-value payments, particularly across borders, automation directly affects how predictable cash flow is, how defensible cost assumptions are, and how much time teams spend reconciling instead of making decisions. This guide looks at how UAE finance teams are approaching payments automation in practice today, where it delivers control, where it often breaks down, and what needs to be designed differently to account for local approval structures, VAT requirements, and cross-border payment realities. Key Takeaways Payments automation changes when finance teams see costs, not how fast money moves. The real advantage comes from approving the financial impact upfront rather than explaining it later. UAE businesses feel automation gaps most in cross-border payments , where FX, settlement timing, and corridor differences quietly erode predictability. Well-designed automation reduces internal friction , not just workload, by aligning finance, procurement, and treasury decisions in a single flow. The strongest automation setups are incremental , starting with high-value suppliers and expanding as controls and data quality stabilise. Platforms like Alaan are designed to move control upstream , combining invoice validation, approvals, FX-aware transfers, and accounting sync into a single, auditable process. Why Automate Business Payments? The Outcomes Finance Leaders Care About Payment automation only matters if it changes outcomes that finance leaders are measured on. In the UAE context, three outcomes stand out. 1. Predictable Cash Flow And FX Exposure For teams paying international suppliers, FX is often treated as a post-payment issue. Rates are accepted at execution, and the true landed cost is reconciled later. Automation changes this by shifting FX visibility before approval , not after settlement. When approvers see the FX impact upfront, payment timing becomes a deliberate decision. That alone reduces variance explanations and makes cash forecasting more defensible in front of management. 2. Faster Processing Without Weaker Controls Automation is often misunderstood as “removing checks.” In practice, the opposite happens. Invoice capture, validation, and routing remove manual steps while tightening control points. Approvals move faster because information is complete, not because standards are lowered. Finance teams that automate invoice intake and approvals typically see fewer exceptions and shorter processing cycles, which directly improves supplier relationships and internal SLAs. 3. Cleaner Month-End And Audit Readiness Every manual handoff creates reconciliation debt. Automated payment workflows reduce this debt by ensuring invoices, approvals, payments, and accounting entries are linked. The benefit shows up at month-end: fewer unmatched items, fewer explanations, and faster closes. The Real Barriers To Payments Automation In UAE Firms Payments automation fails when it ignores how finance teams actually operate in the UAE. The barriers are consistent across industries. 1. Fragmented Systems And Parallel Workflows Invoices arrive by email, approvals happen in messages, accounting sits in an ERP, and payments are executed in bank portals or FX apps. Automation struggles when each step lives in a different tool with no shared context. This fragmentation forces finance teams to manually move data between systems, increasing both processing time and error rates. Until these workflows are connected, automation delivers limited value. 2. Approval Hierarchies And Local Practices Approval culture in UAE organisations is structured and role-based. Payment tools designed for other markets often underestimate this. Systems that cannot reflect real approval hierarchies, delegation rules, or dual-approval requirements are quickly bypassed. Automation must fit existing approval structures , not attempt to replace them. 3. Cross-Border Complexity And Corridor Limitations Many UAE businesses rely on cross-border payments for procurement, imports, or overseas services. Cards often cannot be used, and not all corridors behave the same. FX costs, settlement times, and compliance requirements vary widely. If automation ignores corridor coverage and FX transparency, teams revert to banks or exchange houses for critical payments. 4. Supplier Constraints Some suppliers insist on specific payment formats or timelines. Automation must account for this reality by allowing phased adoption, starting with high-volume suppliers and expanding gradually. Also Read: Understanding Challenges and Complexities in Global E-Invoicing System Practical Strategies To Build Payments Automation That Works Automation succeeds when it is designed upstream and rolled out in controlled stages. The following practices are consistently effective. 1. Capture And Validate Invoices Upstream The fastest way to break a payment process is to let incomplete invoices enter it. High-performing finance teams enforce digital invoice submission to a single intake point. OCR and structured data extraction identify missing fields early, supplier details, invoice numbers, TRNs, and VAT amounts, before approvals begin. A practical rollout starts with the top 20 suppliers by value. This covers most spending while allowing rules to be tested and refined before broader adoption. Related: Understanding E-Invoices in UAE: Purpose, Types, and Elements 2. Separate Invoice Approval From Payment Approval Treating invoice approval and payment approval as the same decision is a common source of rushed payments. Leading teams split the process: Invoice approval confirms validity and coding. Payment approval determines timing, FX exposure, and payment rail. This separation preserves control without slowing execution. Low-risk invoices can move quickly, while high-value or cross-border payments receive appropriate scrutiny. Also Read: Steps to Automate Expense Management and Approvals 3. Surface FX Impact Before Payment Approval For cross-border payments, automation fails if FX is treated as an execution detail. UAE finance teams feel this most when margins are tight and payment sizes are large. Seeing FX differences after settlement turns reconciliation into explanation work. Effective payments automation surfaces FX impact and total landed cost before approval . That means: Approvers see rate, fees, and estimated settlement cost upfront Treasury can decide whether to pay immediately, wait, or use an alternative rail Variances become intentional outcomes, not surprises This single design choice changes behaviour. Payment timing becomes a finance decision rather than an operational reflex. It also simplifies internal reporting. When cost assumptions are approved in advance, explaining deviations to leadership becomes straightforward. Also Read: Building a Robust Cash Management Control System for UAE Businesses 4. Integrate Payments With Accounting For Real-Time Reconciliation Automation that stops at payment execution still leaves work on the table. The real efficiency gain comes when invoice data, approvals, and payments are reflected in accounting without manual intervention . In practice, this means: Invoices post to the ERP with correct VAT treatment Payments automatically close open items Exceptions surface daily instead of at the month-end For finance teams, this removes the CSV loop, exporting from one system, importing into another, and fixing mismatches days later. It also shortens close cycles and reduces audit preparation time. Teams that integrate payments directly with accounting systems tend to catch issues earlier and spend less time reconciling historical data. 5. Use Rules For Recurring And Low-Risk Payments Not every payment deserves the same level of attention. Automation works best when finance teams codify judgment into rules. Common examples: Recurring vendor payments below a defined threshold Approved service contracts with fixed monthly amounts Utilities, subscriptions, or retainers These payments can move through automated flows with audit trails, while one-off or high-value transactions retain manual approval. The result is fewer bottlenecks without sacrificing control. Automation rules also reduce approval fatigue, a quiet but real risk when managers are asked to approve too many low-impact transactions. 6. Track The Right Metrics And Adjust In Short Cycles Automation should be measured operationally, not theoretically. The most useful metrics for UAE finance teams include: Average processing time (invoice received to payment scheduled) Percentage of payments completed within the internal SLA FX variance between approval and settlement Exception rate per 1,000 invoices Volatility in Days Payable Outstanding Teams that review these metrics weekly can adjust rules, approval thresholds, and supplier onboarding quickly. Waiting for quarterly reviews slows learning and adoption. Also Read: How to Post Expenses with VAT in ERP Systems An End-To-End Example: Automated Payments In Practice Consider a UAE-based procurement firm paying overseas suppliers monthly. Suppliers submit digital invoices to a central intake Invoice data is extracted and validated, including VAT and supplier details Department heads approve invoice validity Treasury reviews FX impact and timing before approving payment Payments are executed using the selected rail Entries sync automatically to accounting, closing the loop What changes is not just speed. Finance gains visibilit y into cost assumptions before money moves, reconciliation effort drops, and month-end stops feeling like a recovery exercise. How Alaan Supports Cross-Border Payments Automation In The UAE For many UAE businesses, payment automation challenges surface most clearly when paying international suppliers. Card rails are often unsuitable, and traditional bank or exchange workflows separate invoice review, approval, execution, and reconciliation into different systems. This fragmentation reduces visibility and increases manual work. At Alaan , we support cross-border payments automation by connecting these stages into a governed workflow, so finance teams can review, approve, execute, and reconcile supplier payments within one environment. Super Pay Cross-Border Transfers For Supplier Payments Through SuperPay, Alaan’s transfer capability, we enable domestic and cross-border supplier payments that cannot be handled through card rail. International transfers are currently available across supported corridors, including SEPA-region Europe, India, Pakistan, Egypt, the Philippines, Bangladesh, the United Kingdom, and the United States, with expansion occurring in phases. This allows organisations to execute supplier settlements without shifting between disconnected tools. Visibility Into Cost Before Payment Approval For supported international transfers, payment cost implications are surfaced prior to approval. Finance teams can review this information before deciding when to release funds, helping reduce post-payment surprises and supporting more predictable cash planning. Invoice Capture And Approval Before Execution Invoices enter through a central intake and move through configurable approval chains before any payment is scheduled. This ensures spend validity is confirmed first, and payment timing is considered separately. The structure reflects common finance operating practices in UAE organisations. Accounting Sync After Payment Completion Transfer records and supporting documentation synchronise with accounting integrations, maintaining continuity between payment execution and financial reporting. This reduces manual data handling and helps teams identify reconciliation issues earlier. Corporate Cards For Complementary Operational Spend While supplier settlements typically use transfers, we also provide corporate cards for operational and merchant-based spending, such as employee expenses or digital services. Card activity remains connected to the same approval and accounting workflow, ensuring visibility across different payment types. By structuring cross-border transfers alongside approvals, invoice capture, and accounting sync, we help organisations automate supplier payments without fragmenting governance or documentation. This approach supports clearer oversight as international payment activity grows. Conclusion Business payments automation delivers real value when it improves decision-making, not just execution speed. For UAE finance teams, that means validating invoices before payment, separating approval responsibilities, and understanding cost implications upfront, especially for cross-border transactions. Teams that approach automation this way see fewer surprises, cleaner month-ends, and more predictable cash flow. The gains are operational at first, but they compound into stronger financial control over time. At Alaan , we help finance teams bring invoices, approvals, payments, and reconciliation into one connected workflow, so decisions are made with clarity before money moves. If you want to see how this works in practice for your payment volumes and supplier mix, you can schedule a walkthrough with our team and evaluate it against your current process. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) 1. What is the difference between payment automation and accounts payable automation? Accounts payable automation focuses on invoice intake, validation, and approvals. Payment automation extends further, covering how and when money is released, FX visibility, settlement methods, and reconciliation. In practice, UAE finance teams need to work together to achieve predictable outcomes. 2. Is payment automation suitable for small and mid-sized businesses in the UAE? Yes. Many UAE SMEs adopt payments automation specifically to avoid scaling manual processes. Automation helps smaller teams handle higher transaction volumes, cross-border suppliers, and VAT requirements without adding headcount. 3. How does payment automation impact supplier relationships? When payments are automated correctly, suppliers benefit from faster processing, fewer disputes, and clearer timelines. Consistency in payment execution often improves trust and reduces follow-ups, especially for recurring or overseas vendors. 4. Can automated payment systems handle UAE VAT requirements? Modern automation platforms are designed to support VAT workflows by validating invoice data, capturing VAT amounts, and syncing correctly with accounting systems. However, finance teams should still define internal rules to ensure VAT treatment aligns with their tax advisors’ guidance. 5. What should finance teams evaluate before choosing a payments automation platform? Key factors include approval flexibility, accounting integration depth, cross-border payment coverage, FX transparency, audit trails, and how well the system reflects existing finance controls rather than forcing new ones. 6. How long does it typically take to see value from payments automation? Most UAE finance teams see operational improvements within weeks, particularly in processing time and visibility. Strategic benefits, such as improved cash forecasting and reduced reconciliation effort, tend to compound over the first few closing cycles.

title: How to Invest in Gold for Beginners: A Simple Guide
summary: Want to start investing in gold but don't know where to begin? This beginner-friendly guide breaks down everything you need to know, step by step.
body_text: Personal Finance Gold has been a symbol of wealth for thousands of years, and honestly, it still holds up. Whether you’re watching the news about economic uncertainty or just tired of your savings sitting idle in a low-interest account, you’ve probably wondered: should I be investing in gold? The short answer is, it’s worth seriously considering. And if you’re just starting out, beginner-friendly investment options like gold are a great place to build confidence before diving into riskier assets. The good news? Investing in gold doesn’t have to be complicated or expensive. You don’t need to buy a vault or store bars under your bed. This guide walks you through everything, from why gold matters to exactly how you can start buying it today, no finance degree required. List of Content Toggle Why Gold Is Still a Smart Investment Choice Before we talk about how to invest in gold, let’s talk about why . Understanding the “why” helps you stay committed when markets get bumpy. 1. Gold Holds Its Value Over Time Unlike paper currency, gold doesn’t lose purchasing power to inflation the same way. When inflation rises and currencies weaken, gold tends to hold steady or even increase in value. That’s why many investors treat it as a store of value rather than just a speculative asset. 2. It Diversifies Your Portfolio If stocks and bonds are your main investments, gold adds a layer of protection. It often moves in the opposite direction to the stock market, which means when your equities dip, your gold investment can help cushion the blow. This is called negative correlation , and it’s one of the biggest reasons financial advisors recommend gold as part of a balanced portfolio. 3. High Liquidity Gold is globally recognized and easy to buy or sell almost anywhere in the world. Whether you’re in Jakarta, London, or Dubai, you can convert gold to cash relatively quickly. That kind of liquidity is reassuring, especially in an emergency. Different Ways to Invest in Gold One of the most common misconceptions about gold investing is that you have to physically own it. The truth is, there are several ways to get exposure to gold, and each has its own pros and cons. Here’s a breakdown of the most popular options for beginners. 1. Physical Gold (Bars and Coins) This is the most traditional form of gold investment. You buy gold in physical form, like bars, coins, or even certified bullion, and store it yourself or in a secure facility. It feels tangible and real, which many investors love. The downside is that you need to think about safe storage and insurance. If you’re interested in this route, it’s worth learning how to save gold through institutions like Pegadaian , which makes the whole process much simpler and more accessible. 2. Gold Jewelry Buying gold jewelry is one of the most popular ways people accumulate gold, especially in Southeast Asia. It’s practical and wearable. However, jewelry typically comes with a making charge (the cost of crafting), which means you’re paying more than the raw gold value. When you sell it, you usually only get paid for the gold content. If you’re considering this route, read up on whether gold jewelry investment is truly profitable before committing. 3. Gold ETFs (Exchange-Traded Funds) Gold ETFs let you invest in gold without physically owning it. You buy shares in a fund that tracks the price of gold, and those shares are traded on the stock exchange just like regular stocks. It’s a great option if you want exposure to gold prices without dealing with storage. You’ll need a brokerage account to get started. 4. Digital Gold Many fintech platforms now let you buy digital gold , where your purchase is backed by real physical gold stored securely in a vault. You can start with very small amounts, sometimes as little as the equivalent of a cup of coffee. It’s convenient, flexible, and perfect for beginners who want to start small and grow gradually. 5. Gold Mining Stocks and Mutual Funds Another indirect way to invest in gold is by buying shares in gold mining companies or gold-focused mutual funds. These can offer higher returns, but they also come with higher risk since you’re exposed to both gold prices and company performance. This is generally better suited for investors who already have some experience. Step-by-Step: How to Start Investing in Gold Ready to take action? Here’s a simple process to get started, no matter which method you choose. 1. Set Your Financial Goals First Before buying any gold, ask yourself: what is this investment for? Emergency fund backup? Long-term wealth building? Protecting against inflation? Knowing your goal helps you decide how much to invest and which method fits best. It also helps to have a solid handle on your finances first. Tracking your income and expenses is a great first step to figure out how much you can comfortably set aside for investing. 2. Start Small and Be Consistent You don’t need a large lump sum to start. In fact, many experts recommend a dollar-cost averaging approach, where you invest a fixed amount regularly (weekly or monthly) regardless of the current price. This smooths out price volatility over time and removes the pressure of trying to “time the market.” 3. Choose a Trusted Platform or Institution Whether you’re buying physical gold, digital gold, or ETFs, always use a reputable, well-known platform or institution. Look for clear documentation, proper receipts, and transparent pricing. If you’re using a digital platform, check that your gold purchases are backed by actual physical gold stored in a certified vault. 4. Think About Storage and Security If you own physical gold, storage is a real concern. Home safes are an option, but for larger amounts, consider renting a safety deposit box at a bank or using a custodial service. If you’re investing through digital platforms or ETFs, this concern is mostly handled for you, which is another reason many beginners prefer those routes. 5. Monitor, But Don’t Obsess Gold is a long-term investment . Its value can fluctuate in the short term, so don’t panic if you see a dip right after you buy. Check in periodically, but don’t glue yourself to price charts every day. The real power of gold comes from holding it over years, not days. Common Mistakes Beginners Make with Gold Learning from other people’s mistakes is one of the best shortcuts in investing. Here are the most common pitfalls to avoid. Putting all your money into gold: Gold is a diversifier, not a get-rich-quick scheme. Keep it as part of a broader investment strategy. Buying from unverified sellers: Fake gold is a real problem. Always buy from certified dealers or reputable platforms. Ignoring the buy-sell spread: The price you buy at and the price you can sell at are not the same. Factor this into your planning. Panic selling during dips: Short-term drops are normal. Selling in a panic locks in losses that would have recovered over time. Skipping research on jewelry: If you’re buying gold jewelry as an investment, always check the purity (measured in karats) and the actual gold weight before purchasing. How Gold Fits Into Your Bigger Financial Picture Gold works best when it’s part of a broader, balanced financial plan. Think of it as one pillar of your financial house, not the whole structure. Pair it with a healthy emergency fund, consistent savings habits, and other investment vehicles to build real long-term security. If you’re looking for a practical foundation to build on, check out this practical guide on how to save money before scaling up your investments. For those working abroad or managing money across borders, it’s also worth exploring how gold fits into an expat financial strategy. Combining smart savings, gold investments, and efficient money transfers can make a real difference to your long-term wealth. You can find some great ideas in this guide on saving and investment strategies while working in Malaysia . See Also: Easy and Practical Investment Options for Stay-at-Home Moms Gold investing is one of those things that sounds intimidating at first but becomes surprisingly straightforward once you understand the basics. Start with a clear goal, pick a method that fits your lifestyle, stay consistent, and give it time. Whether you’re stacking physical bars or accumulating digital gold a little each month, you’re building a habit that your future self will thank you for. Now go ahead and take that first step. title: How to Choose an Employee Experience Platform: The Ultimate Guide for HR Teams
summary: Learn what an employee experience platform is, its key features, benefits, integrations, pricing, and how to evaluate the right platform for your organization.
body_text: What Is an Employee Experience Platform and Why HR Teams Need One Most HR teams operate with a collection of disconnected systems. Employees open one tool for payroll, another for benefits, a third for company news, and yet another to find colleagues. This fragmentation creates friction at every touchpoint. The change from traditional HR tools to experience platforms Enterprise work has become more connected, though many organizations still work through fragmented tools and information. Employees move between messaging apps, knowledge bases, HR systems, and collaboration tools just to find what they need to do their jobs. Momentum slows when the employee experience feels disconnected. Important updates get missed. Knowledge becomes harder to find. New hires take longer to ramp. The pressure on organizations has intensified. 73% of HR leaders feel that management doesn't have the right tools, resources, or knowledge to work through these changes, according to Gartner's 2024 annual HR Priorities survey. Teams become disconnected without solid communication and clear organization-wide visibility. Departmental coordination suffers, and employee disengagement follows. Traditional HR tools were built for specific functions. Your HRIS manages payroll and compliance. Your learning management system hosts training content. Your survey tool captures feedback. Each serves its purpose, but none addresses how these systems work together to shape daily employee experience. HR teams spend cycles reconciling reports rather than acting on insights. How EXPs differ from HRIS and intranets An employee experience platform is a digital workplace layer that brings the systems employees rely on into one cohesive experience. It connects internal communication, knowledge access, collaboration, business tools, and workflow support so employees can move through work with less friction. The difference matters. An HRIS is a system of record. It stores employment data, manages payroll and benefits administration, and tracks compliance. Your HRIS handles structured HR data but wasn't designed for daily communication, knowledge discovery, or cultural engagement. Employees use HR systems transactionally to complete tasks, access records, or deal with specific HR moments. Intranets emerged as document repositories and one-way broadcast channels. They stored policies, org charts, and news, but interaction was minimal. Employees visited to find a form, then left. Content often became stale, and engagement was an afterthought. An employee experience platform is a system of engagement . It supports the full employee journey, from onboarding and training to daily execution, recognition, development, and change communication. A strong employee experience platform helps enterprises deliver the right information, tools, and next steps at the right time. Personalization makes the experience more relevant, while system integrations make it easier to use. The operational difference shows up daily. Organizations that prioritize employee experience see an 18% lift in productivity, thanks to efficient processes and reduced friction. Companies with strategic employee engagement programs experience up to 51% lower attrition rates. These platforms free up HR teams and IT teams by automating routine support tasks and allow them to focus on strategic initiatives. Core components that define a modern EXP Modern employee experience platforms share specific capabilities that distinguish them from simple intranet solutions. AI-powered search and discovery stands as one of the clearest signals of platform quality. Friction spreads when employees struggle to find policies, updates, training, or knowledge. A modern platform should make discovery feel more intuitive with AI-powered enterprise search that helps employees surface relevant results faster. Personalized communication transforms how information reaches people. Enterprise communication works better when it reflects role, location, language, business unit, and employee context. A modern employee experience platform acts as a personalized communication layer and gives employees one place to see company news, local updates, leadership messages, and task-relevant content without flooding everyone with the same feed. Collaboration workspaces create continuity between communication, teamwork, and knowledge sharing. Teams need spaces to share information, coordinate work, and maintain context. Recognition should feel visible, timely, and easy to participate in. Platforms that support peer acknowledgment and milestone celebrations help reinforce appreciation across the organization. Strong analytics help teams move from assumptions to evidence. That means understanding what employees search for, which content performs well, how communication reaches different groups, and where adoption stalls. A platform improves remote team experience when employees can access it in the moments that matter. Mobile accessibility helps connect distributed workforce management by giving employees easier access to updates, resources, and everyday tools wherever work happens. Integration capabilities often determine platform strength. That means collaboration suites, HR systems, identity providers, document repositories, service tools, and business applications. Workflow automation helps reduce manual effort and supports more consistent experiences across common processes. Employee experience is shaped by everyday moments as much as major milestones. Understanding Your Organization's Specific EX Needs Selecting an employee experience platform without understanding what you need wastes investment and kills adoption. Get into where your current approach falls short and what your organization genuinely requires before you evaluate vendors or request demos. Assess your current employee engagement tools gaps Only 20% of employees worldwide and 31% in the U.S. fall under the "engaged" category. Most organizations struggle to create conditions where employees feel emotionally connected to their work. This gap signals trouble. Research reveals engaged employees achieve 23% higher profitability and 18% higher productivity in sales when you compare the most engaged teams to the least engaged. They also show 51% less turnover in low-turnover organizations. Audit what you use now. Many HR teams rely on separate systems for surveys, recognition, communication and performance tracking. You cannot see patterns when things are fragmented. Your survey tool might show declining engagement, but if it sits disconnected from your recognition platform and performance data, you cannot identify whether lack of appreciation or unclear expectations drives the decline. Check whether your existing employee engagement tools capture meaningful data. Questions that link to performance outcomes are what you need to measure engagement. Your tools should help managers structure coaching conversations and performance reviews. They should track elements like clarity, resources and recognition. Drive follow-up action rather than just collecting data. Identify pain points in the employee's lifecycle Employee interactions span multiple experiential phases from candidacy to alumni status. Each transitional milestone presents renewed needs and priorities that need attention. Specific lifecycle moments carry disproportionate emotional and commercial impact. Pain points often concentrate there. Onboarding represents one critical moment. Only 1 in 10 employees strongly agree their organization does a great job of onboarding new hires. 28% of employees leave their new jobs within the first 90 days, often due to poor onboarding or mismatched expectations. A strong onboarding process can improve new hire retention by 82% and productivity by over 70%. Development and growth opportunities surface as another frequent pain point. Lack of career growth ranks as the top reason employees leave organizations. 63% of workers who quit cite lack of advancement opportunities as a reason for leaving. 94% would stay at a company longer if it invested in their career development when employees see a path forward and feel supported in learning new skills. Map your current employee lifecycle to identify where friction occurs. Track speed of capability build during onboarding and engagement scores from early feedback surveys. Monitor program participation rates that reflect buy-in. Check attrition rates mapped to tenure brackets and exit interview feedback loop completion rates. Map requirements for distributed workforce management Traditional tools cannot address the unique challenges that distributed work introduces. A distributed workforce consists of team members spread over various locations who work remotely to achieve common goals. Success requires communication, collaboration and unity that surpass geographical boundaries. Common distributed workforce challenges include lack of face-to-face communication where team members miss nonverbal cues. Live collaboration becomes complex when different locations and time zones are involved. Over-dependency on written communication causes hindrances. Cultural differences lead to misinterpretations. Building personal relationships remotely becomes difficult and impacts team cohesion and trust. Your platform requirements should address these specific needs. Think about whether the solution supports asynchronous communication to accommodate different time zones and work schedules. Check if it provides mobile accessibility for remote team experience. Does it enable transparent documentation so information remains available whatever the location? Does it aid regular feedback mechanisms and integrate with communication tools your distributed teams already use? Organizations managing distributed workforces benefit from AI HR technology that can automate routine communications. It surfaces relevant knowledge based on context and personalizes information delivery based on role and location. Think about your tech stack and integration needs A well-laid-out HR tech stack improves productivity and effectiveness. It decreases costs and simplifies processes. Survey data shows the average organization uses about 21 HR solutions, up from around 10 in 2019. You waste enormous time and productivity when you enter the same information in multiple platforms without proper integration. Map your current systems first. Most large organizations use multiple systems including core HR or HCM platforms and payroll and time management systems. They also use recruitment and applicant tracking systems, learning and development platforms, performance and talent management tools, and people analytics software. Assess compatibility with these existing systems. Your employee experience platform should offer single sign-on capabilities and reliable APIs for data flow between systems. Look for either native integrations or middleware options to connect best-of-breed tools. Companies that relied on only one HR platform saw nearly 70% of employees report confidence in finding needed information. Those using multiple platforms saw only 49% confidence. Integration eliminates data silos and improves accuracy and compliance by keeping information consistent. It saves time by automating repetitive tasks and boosts employee experience through smooth single-portal access. Better analytics become possible by connecting data throughout the employee's lifecycle. Essential Features Every Employee Experience Platform Should Have Feature requirements vary in organizations, but certain capabilities remain non-negotiable for any platform claiming to improve employee experience. These core functions determine whether your investment translates into measurable improvements or becomes another underutilized system. Communication and knowledge management capabilities A centralized communication hub replaces mass emails and scattered announcements with targeted messaging that reaches the right people at the right time. Effective platforms offer audience targeting by role, location, and language so employees see what matters to them. Channels for structured internal updates and announcements keep remote and hybrid teams aligned with scheduled posting and targeted distribution. Knowledge management transforms how employees find and use information in systems. Structured pages for policies, how-to guides, onboarding hubs, and team spaces provide access to critical resources in an organized way. Version control and content governance prevent outdated information from confusing employees. Enterprise search in intranet content, people directory, documents, and integrated tools ensures employees find answers in seconds, not minutes. Employee engagement tools and feedback systems Platforms offer tools to conduct surveys, polls, and pulse checks to gather valuable employee insights. This enables businesses to gage sentiment and identify areas to improve. These feedback mechanisms provide up-to-the-minute responses on matters affecting the business and the team. Anonymous feedback options combined with short, frequent pulse surveys create a continuous data stream that gives businesses a constant pulse on employee sentiment. The ability to capture feedback throughout the employee lifecycle matters just as much. Event-triggered or time-based surveys synced with your HRIS allow you to improve every stage of the employee journey and act before problems escalate. Recognition and rewards functionality Recognition systems allow you to recognize and reward employee achievements. This promotes a culture of appreciation and boosts morale. Peer-to-peer recognition platforms enable employees to acknowledge and reward colleagues for their contributions. Public recognition feeds, social recognition tied to company values, and gratitude tracking encourage frequent appreciation. Reward catalogs include gift cards, experiences, charitable donations, and points-based systems that give employees flexibility while offering HR leaders budget control. Organizations running global recognition programs benefit from platforms supporting rewards in 100+ countries. AI powered employee experience platform capabilities AI HR technology delivers personalized, up-to-the-minute support by surfacing relevant content based on employee intent and automating routine tasks to streamline workflows. AI-powered search understands context and intent rather than just keywords. This helps employees surface relevant results faster. Conversational AI assistants answer questions directly from authorized content and support hands-free interaction for factory, logistics, and retail environments. AI assists with content creation through on-brand rewrites and translations in 75 or more languages with unified analytics. Sentiment analysis measures how employees felt about communications, not just whether they opened them. Mobile accessibility for remote team experience Full-featured mobile apps for iOS and Android support deskless and frontline workers who cannot access platforms from job sites or retail floors. Mobile-first design ensures functionality works well on devices. Frontline employees access information primarily through personal smartphones. QR code authentication, employee ID login, and offline mode capabilities allow employees to securely access content without corporate email addresses or constant connectivity. Analytics and reporting dashboards Dashboards showing reach, engagement, search behavior, and channel performance guide communications and HR strategy with useful insights. Analytics segmented by channel, team, location, and role reveal which sites or populations aren't being reached rather than relying on total averages. Platforms tracking what employees search for, which content performs well, and where adoption stalls provide early signals of confusion, disengagement, or knowledge gaps. How to Evaluate Platform Integration and Compatibility Integration determines whether your employee experience platform becomes a unified hub or another isolated tool employees need to work around. The technical architecture behind your platform choice affects everything from daily user experience to long-term scalability. Assessing compatibility with existing HR systems Application programming interfaces (APIs) make data exchange seamless across all the different connection points in an interdependent digital ecosystem. APIs enable diverse applications to connect smoothly and share data between systems with ease. To cite an instance, when an employee gets married, that information should be shared with the benefits system because the new marital status could result in a change in benefits coverage. The average organization now has 11 systems of record. More than 70% of companies have legacy systems and multiple cloud HCM platforms. Your employee experience platform needs to bridge this heterogeneous environment without forcing you to rebuild your entire tech stack. Assess whether vendors offer pre-built integrations with your core systems. Organizations with 40+ out-of-the-box integrations provide stronger integration capabilities than those requiring custom development for each connection. Integration value extends beyond convenience. Mid-sized companies found that integrations prevented churn by 70-79%. Small companies reported a 50-59% effect. When you evaluate compatibility, get into how the platform handles employee data synchronization with your HRIS. Check whether it can pull organizational hierarchy for personalized content delivery and if it supports bidirectional data flow for cases requiring updates across multiple systems. Single sign-on and data flow requirements Single sign-on (SSO) lets users sign in once and reach many applications. With SSO, users sign in with one set of credentials and can then open every assigned application without signing in again. SSO works based upon a trust relationship set up between an application, known as the service provider, and an identity provider. When an employee tries to access a different website, the new website would have to have a similar trust relationship configured with the SSO solution. Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) 2.0 is a mature, XML-based standard used widely in enterprises and suits traditional web apps. OpenID Connect (OIDC) is a modern protocol built on OAuth 2.0 that uses JSON-based tokens and suits modern web apps, mobile apps, and APIs that need both authentication and authorization. Data flow patterns matter just as much. APIs enable real-time, automatic data syncing. When an organization hires a new employee, HR can enter the employee's information into one system of record. An API then sends that data to other systems, such as time tracking or learning management, without any manual work. Tech firm HR solutions and API capabilities Tech firm HR solutions rely heavily on API quality to enable customer-facing integrations. Integrations are the third most important factor for B2B buyers globally, followed by trust and sales flexibility. Only 29% of HR tech users say the components of their HR tech stack integrate well. This causes the average mid-sized company to replace 39% of their SaaS applications with ones that have better functionality and integration offerings. Evaluate API documentation quality, rate limits, and webhook support for event-driven workflows. Strong APIs provide all the building blocks that a developer needs to integrate two or more systems with each other. Cloud-based vs on-premise considerations Cloud solutions spread costs over time with monthly or annual subscriptions. On-premise requires a big upfront investment in hardware, software licenses, and implementation services. Cloud intranets launch quickly, with setup taking hours to days. On-premise deployments take months. For distributed workforce management, cloud-based platforms are designed from the ground up to be accessed from anywhere with an internet connection. On-premise systems can support remote access, but it requires additional infrastructure and can be more complex to manage securely. Cloud vendors maintain SOC 2 and ISO 27001 certifications, hold industry-specific attestations, apply security patches continuously, and monitor infrastructure around the clock. On-premise only makes sense for classified environments, strict data sovereignty requirements, or existing infrastructure investments. Comparing Vendor Offerings and Pricing Models Vendor pricing varies dramatically in the employee experience platform market. Direct comparisons prove challenging without understanding what drives those differences. Understanding different pricing structures Pricing models split into several distinct categories. Per-seat monthly pricing remains most common, where costs scale with user count. Platforms like monday service charge INR 2,193.89 per seat monthly for standard plans and INR 3,206.46 for professional tiers. Zendesk follows similar patterns, with suite team plans at INR 4,640.92 per agent monthly and enterprise reaching INR 14,260.30. Microsoft Viva takes a modular approach and bundles communications and communities at INR 168.76 per user monthly while workplace analytics runs INR 506.28 monthly. Quote-based pricing dominates enterprise solutions where customization drives costs. ServiceNow, Workday, and similar tech firm HR solutions require formal assessment before revealing pricing, as costs depend on deployment scope, user populations, and module selection. This opacity complicates budgeting but reflects the reality that implementations vary widely in organizations of all sizes. Total cost of ownership beyond licensing fees The quoted price reflects only licensing, often the smallest portion of total ownership cost. Total cost of ownership analysis combines upfront costs with ongoing and hidden costs that accumulate over the product or service's lifespan. Acquisition costs include purchase price, licensing fees, setup and implementation costs, and hardware or software investments. Operating costs cover ongoing expenses such as IT labor, administrative time, and subscription fees. Maintenance and support costs cover repairs, upgrades, vendor support, and training. Indirect costs frequently exceed visible expenses. Downtime and productivity losses drain budgets without visibility. Organizations focusing only on sticker price see total costs rise by 15-20% once invisible expenses kick in. Implementation and support services included Implementation timelines affect costs. Cloud intranets launch fast, with simple setup taking hours to days, while on-premise deployments take months. Vendor support quality determines whether issues resolve fast or linger. Assess whether onboarding assistance, ongoing maintenance, and training resources come bundled or require separate contracts. Scalability as your organization grows Platform costs for employee experience platforms can range from a few hundred dollars to several thousand dollars each year, determined based on the full scope of what the company needs and the platform's level of support for customizations. Assess whether pricing structures accommodate growth without penalty. Some vendors charge per user, while others offer volume discounts at scale. Testing Platforms Through Demos and Pilot Programs Vendor selection decisions carry too much weight to rely on marketing materials and feature checklists alone. Demos, trials, and proofs of concept move you beyond promises to see how platforms perform with your team. What to look for in vendor demonstrations Research shows 62% of software purchasers rank product trials as a top factor in final purchase decisions, while 54% prioritize product demos. Demos provide your first chance to see platforms in action and spot what they can and cannot do before committing. Most demonstrations follow a predictable structure: vendor overview and platform philosophy, live walkthrough of core features, branding and customization options, integration capabilities, security details, and support services. You need your must-haves and challenges defined before the demo. Write down the main capabilities you need and keep them visible during the demo so you maintain focus. Involve stakeholders from IT, HR, and communications who contributed to your shortlist, as they have vendor-specific questions. Ask vendors to demonstrate real-life user experiences rather than just features. Request they show how a new hire in a specific location finds everything needed on day one, how a manager publishes a targeted security update and captures acknowledgements, or how employees locate policies and complete requests in under 30 seconds. Running effective pilot programs with real users Standard trials offer self-guided learning of out-of-the-box features. Proofs of concept provide tailored test environments with your branding, workflows, and vendor support. POCs verify that platforms can solve your unique challenges before you commit, especially valuable when you have specific integrations to test, stakeholder buy-in to secure, or complex requirements to handle. POCs run 2-4 weeks and include a dedicated test environment, customization that reflects real use cases, vendor training and checkpoints, success objectives, and regular feedback sessions. Preparation determines POC value. You need to outline expectations and use cases, assemble a project lead with representatives from IT, HR, communications, and end users, gather brand assets and sample content, allocate time for training and testing, and clarify vendor requirements including agreements and integration coordination. Gathering feedback from HR teams and employees Keep your search team focused and participating rather than overwhelmed. Assign different roles and permissions that mimic real scenarios, test actual tasks your team will perform rather than just learning features, document feedback as issues arise, and stay on schedule with agreed timelines and checkpoints. Measuring adoption and engagement during trials Positive indicators include stakeholder engagement with active participation and questions, smooth onboarding where users access platforms after training with ease, platform reliability with quick issue resolution, successful customization that reflects organizational needs, use case validation without major roadblocks, vendor communication that stays clear, applicable feedback that informs decisions, and measurable progress against objectives. Building Your Business Case and Getting Stakeholder Buy-In Securing executive approval requires you to demonstrate financial effect, not just operational benefits. Finance teams and senior leaders assess proposals through return metrics, risk evaluation, and strategic arrangement. Calculating ROI and expected outcomes ROI calculations translate employee experience platform investments into measurable financial outcomes. The simple formula multiplies total benefits minus total costs, divided by total costs, then converted to percentage. Organizations that implement employee engagement tools see improving employee engagement by up to 20%. This contributes to 311% ROI. This improvement produces a 1.5% increase in profitability and a 20% increase in manager and HR team productivity. Attrition and related costs decrease by 5%. Turnover reduction delivers the clearest financial effect. Replacement costs average 20% of annual salary. These costs cover recruitment fees, screening, hiring manager time, onboarding programs, and productivity ramp periods. Organizations save substantial amounts each year by reducing attrition just 5%. An organization with 8,825 full-time equivalents experiencing 25% annual turnover replaces 2,206 employees yearly at a most important cost. Presenting the case to leadership and finance Stakeholder mapping identifies who holds approval authority versus who influences decisions. Create three deliverables: a one-page executive summary highlighting ROI and strategic fit, a detailed business case document with full analysis and supporting data, and a seven-slide presentation. The presentation should cover the chance statement, alternatives you considered, cost-benefit summary, your recommendation, risks, milestones, and closing statement. Addressing common objections and concerns Budget concerns require you to reframe cost as investment. When stakeholders question expense, demonstrate how the ai powered employee experience platform reduces costs elsewhere. Decreased turnover, improved productivity, and simplified processes make this possible. Timing objections surface when competing priorities exist. Counter by showing the costs of delay and how distributed workforce management challenges worsen without intervention. Need validation requires you to connect platform capabilities to documented pain points from your assessment phase. Implementation Planning and Change Management Once approval is secured, implementation quality determines whether your employee experience platform delivers promised returns or becomes another underutilized system. Creating a realistic rollout timeline Phased rollouts prove more effective than big-bang launches. Start with one department facing most important challenges or showing eagerness for change. Each phase should run 30-60-90 day cycles. This allows you to test, gather feedback and adjust before expanding. The approach reduces risk and builds momentum through visible wins. Training plans for HR teams and managers Manager enablement separates successful platforms from failed ones. Managers account for 70% of the variance in team-level engagement, which makes their adoption critical. Training should extend beyond the launch. Hold regular refresher sessions when analytics reveal low content visits from specific departments. Continuous learning will give capabilities that match evolving platform features. Communication strategy for employee adoption Multi-channel communication reaches employees where they work. Combine short alerts via email, Teams or digital signage with detailed content on the platform itself. For distributed workforce management, mobile-first access will give frontline workers updates on par with others. Executive visibility matters as well. Employees follow when leadership uses the platform. Measuring success and continuous improvement Track metrics linking to business outcomes rather than vanity numbers. Monitor first-contact resolution rates and employee satisfaction scores across different segments. Review data at 30, 60 and 90 days. Adjust strategy based on actual usage patterns. Conclusion You now have what you need to select the right employee experience platform for your organization. We've covered how to assess your unique needs, evaluate key features, test platforms with real users, and build a strong business case for leadership. Success depends on matching platform capabilities to your actual pain points rather than chasing feature lists. Involve stakeholders, run pilots, and plan implementation with care. The right platform changes how employees connect with work and each other. Start with a clear picture of where friction exists today. Then choose the solution that addresses those specific challenges. Your investment will pay off through stronger involvement, lower turnover, and measurably better output.

body_text: View All News Entegris Reports Results for Second Quarter of 2026 Aug 4, 2026 Download (opens in new window) Net sales of $883 million. GAAP diluted EPS of $0.61. Non-GAAP diluted EPS of $0.93. BILLERICA, Mass.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Entegris, Inc. (NASDAQ: ENTG), today reported its financial results for the Company’s second quarter ended June 27, 2026. Dave Reeder, Entegris’ President and Chief Executive Officer, said: “We delivered another strong quarter, exceeding our guidance across all key metrics as improving semiconductor demand and accelerating customer capital investments drove double-digit growth across both our unit and capex-related businesses. Our operational initiatives continued to enhance profitability and cash generation, further strengthening our financial position. title: The Best Shapewear for Hip Dips, Ranked (2026)
summary: Discover the best shapewear for smoothing hip dips, from Honeylove’s SuperPower Short to briefs designed for shorter hemlines and sculpted curves.
body_text: Honeylove offers five levels of support, and the Queen Brief is a level four: Strong Support garment. Reviewers highlight its ability to compress where it's needed while avoiding the "jelly roll" effect at the top of the waistband. Best for: Weddings, formal events, and occasion wear where a more structured, lingerie-adjacent aesthetic is wanted alongside the shaping function. #4 Leonisa PowerStay Seamless Short: Best stay-put option What earns the Leonisa PowerStay a spot on this list is a single, specific engineering choice: anti-slip grip technology at the waistband for no roll-down. When shapewear rolls at the waist, it bunches right at the hip dip zone and makes the indentation worse. The PowerStay's grip construction addresses that failure mode directly. At $55, you get: AirFlex™ compression fabric. Made of Leonisa's signature super-soft AirFlex™ fabric for comfortable compression. Specialty stay-in-place waistband. Designed to stay in place, with built-in compression to shape the tummy and waist. Laser-cut leg bands. Go completely invisible under tight dresses or fitted pants. Ruched back seam. Offers a butt-lifting effect. S–XXL, Brown/Nude and Black Reviewers praise the lightweight feel and breathability for all-day wear. The anti-slip waistband earns genuine appreciation across reviews. The tradeoffs worth knowing: roll-down is still flagged in some Amazon reviews, particularly in smaller sizes and specific colorways. The specialty waistband grip works well for some body types and not others. Some reviewers also note seams are visible under very tight or structured clothing. Best for: The reader who prioritizes stay-put construction and a second-skin feel over firm compression, for everyday wear under fitted clothing. #5 Miraclesuit Shape with an Edge Thigh Slimmer: Best for extra firm control The Miraclesuit earns the firm-control position because it holds nothing back. It delivers maximum compression for the tummy, hips, thighs, and rear, with a triple-ply tummy control panel for targeted shaping. At $63, the construction includes: Extra firm compression. Maximum compression transforms your midriff, tummy, waist, and hips. Wonderful Edge® silicone leg openings. A silicone edge on the leg openings won't ride up or roll, eliminates visible lines, and stays comfortable all day. Back-center seam. Provides extra definition for a curved rear, while the high-waist design prevents muffin top. S–3XL Reviewers consistently praise the Wonderful Edge silicone band for keeping the leg openings in place. One reviewer preferred the firm control and fit over a competing Spanx product, noting the top stays put in front and back and the legs stay put as well. The tradeoffs here are significant. There is no slit or hook-and-eye in the gusset, meaning you'd have to remove your dress and the shapewear entirely to use the bathroom. Multiple reviewers flag this as a major inconvenience, especially under formal gowns. Durability is also a concern: some reviewers report ripping at the inner thigh seam after limited wear. Best for: Event wear where maximum compression and the Wonderful Edge® leg construction are worth the durability and bathroom-access tradeoff. #6 Commando Classic Control Short: Best for everyday light wear Commando earns the light-wear slot through material quality and invisible construction. The Classic Control Short is built from European microfiber with raw-cut, seamless edges that eliminate visible lines, elastic digs, and trim marks that plague most shapewear under fitted clothing. At $64, the build is straightforward: Raw-cut edges. No elastic, no trim, no taping. This eliminates digs and visible panty lines entirely. Light-to-moderate compression. Smoothing, not reshaping. XS–3X Reviewers consistently praise how invisible the shorts are under clothing. The raw-cut edges and thin fabric mean no lines under dresses or fitted pants, making them a favorite for everyday layering. Comfort is the dominant positive theme, with multiple reviewers describing barely noticing they're wearing them. The tradeoffs: roll-down at the waistband is the most consistent negative pattern in reviews. The word "control" oversells the compression level. These smooth, but they don't reshape. If you need firm lateral hold at the outer hip, you'll need more structure. Best for: Everyday wear under looser hemlines when you want seamless, invisible smoothing without significant compression. Not for event wear where all-day hold under a fitted dress is the priority. #7 Yummie Ultralight Shapewear Short: Best budget shapewear for hip dips At $20, the Yummie Ultralight is honest about what it is. If you need anti-chafe coverage and a clean silhouette under a casual dress without spending $80+, it delivers on that promise. The box includes: Light shaping. Yummie calls it a "Yummie Hug." Don't expect firm compression. 4" wide 2-ply waistband, high rise Silicone strip at leg hem. Designed to prevent riding up. Seamless side construction S/M–2X/3X Reviewers praise the lightweight, breathable feel for all-day wear, even in heat. The silicone leg band earns appreciation for keeping the hem in place. Multiple reviewers describe it as solid value for light coverage under casual dresses. The tradeoffs are real. Roll-down at the waist is the dominant complaint, repeated heavily across reviews and sizes. The silicone leg band anchors the bottom, but the waistband has no equivalent grip. Compression is genuinely light. The leg band can be visible under very fitted clothing, and sizing inconsistency crops up across colorways. Best for: The reader on a budget who needs anti-chafe coverage and light smoothing under casual dresses. Honeylove: The best shapewear for hip dips Honeylove wins because the brand engineers their garments to target the outer hip. Compression panels are placed where you'd actually want more hold — across the stomach and around the outer hip — with less compression in areas where you need flexibility or movement. The targeted midsection compression panel delivers shaping and coverage to areas that other shapewear ignores. The flexible side-seam boning solves the structural anchoring problem that makes most shapewear roll. If your shapewear smooths the front but does nothing for the outer hip, the issue isn't your body. It's the shaping garment. Honeylove's Sizing Tool can help you match the right silhouette to your outfit and body so you get lateral coverage where you actually need it. Best shapewear for hip dips FAQs Does shapewear minimize hip dips? Yes, but only if the garment applies compression laterally at the outer hip, not just across the front. Shapewear built around front-only tummy panels won't reach the dip zone. Look for garments with side-panel compression and structural boning that defines the waist above the dip. Should I wear a brief or a short for hip dips? It depends on your hemline. Shorts cover the full outer hip-to-thigh curve and work best under midi and maxi dresses, fitted trousers, and bodycon skirts. Briefs deliver the same waist-and-hip engineering but end higher, making them the right choice for above-the-knee skirts and shorter hemlines where a short's leg band would show. Why does my shapewear make my hip dips look worse? Two common reasons. The garment compresses the front without holding the sides, pushing volume laterally into the dip zone. Or the waistband rolls down and bunches at the outer hip, creating an extra ridge right where the dip is. Shapewear with flexible side boning and zoned lateral compression prevents both failure modes.

title: Quantinuum and Oracle Partner to Accelerate Hybrid Quantum Compute Adoption on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure
summary: Quantinuum and Oracle aim to support enterprise, AI lab, academic, and research applications spanning drug discovery, materials science, financial modeling, and large-scale optimization, including AI workloads.
body_text: Broomfield, Colorado and Austin, Texas—Aug 11, 2026 Quantinuum (NASDAQ: QNT), a leading quantum computing company, and Oracle today announced a multi-year strategic partnership to bring quantum computing to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI). Under the partnership, OCI customers will be able to directly access Quantinuum’s Helios , the most accurate commercial quantum computer in the world,1 through OCI’s quantum service, alongside OCI’s high-performance computing (HPC) and GPU infrastructure. Together, Quantinuum and Oracle plan to explore how hybrid quantum-AI infrastructure could address some of the most computationally intensive challenges facing enterprises and broaden access for universities and research institutions advancing scientific discovery and education. The partnership reflects a shared vision that the future of enterprise computing will be built on the convergence of AI, classical supercomputing, and quantum computing. Many complex problems across materials discovery, drug development, logistics, energy, and financial modeling already push the limits of today’s computing architectures. “We believe the next phase of enterprise computing will be shaped by bringing quantum, AI, and high-performance computing together,” said Dr. Rajeeb Hazra, President and CEO of Quantinuum . “Deploying Helios inside OCI gives Quantinuum and Oracle an opportunity to create a unique and deeply integrated environment for hybrid workloads, explore enterprise use cases with customers, and accelerate commercial adoption.” Quantum computing offers a fundamentally different approach to computation with the potential to address problems that are impractical for traditional systems alone. In addition, quantum computing uses significantly less energy than supercomputers. A single Helios system has an estimated power draw of less than one percent of the draw reported for leading supercomputers,2 offering a lower power complementary resource for suitable hybrid workloads. “AI has changed what organizations can imagine, and we believe quantum computing can expand what they’re able to solve,” said Mahesh Thiagarajan, Executive Vice President of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure . “By bringing Quantinuum’s Helios to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, we want to give developers a practical and secure way to explore how quantum computing could complement their existing AI and HPC workloads on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure while improving compute efficiency and energy use.” With Quantinuum’s Helios on OCI, customers can expect to gain managed, secure access to cloud-hosted quantum computing without having to procure, install, or operate dedicated hardware or specialized facilities. Helios, launched commercially in November 2025, is Quantinuum’s third-generation quantum computer. The 98-physical-qubit trapped-ion system has been used in demonstrations involving 48 logical qubits and achieves an average two-qubit gate fidelity of 99.921%, exceeding the widely cited “three 9s” threshold. Helios is designed for hybrid integration with classical HPC and AI environments. By operating on-premises within OCI’s infrastructure, Helios is anticipated to be able to integrate seamlessly with existing OCI compute, networking, storage, identity, and data services under the same governance and access controls customers already use. Oracle plans to preview its OCI quantum service in the coming months, giving developers a streamlined way to move from simulation to execution on real quantum computing hardware. The planned OCI quantum service is expected to combine Quantinuum’s development stack with support for open-source hybrid-programming frameworks, helping developers build, test, and refine quantum-classical applications more efficiently. New Possibilities for Hybrid Quantum-AI Computing “Our roadmap includes exploring classical-quantum hybrid computing to accelerate scientific discovery,” said Johannes Blaschke, Head of Scientific Computing, GBI at Ellison Institute of Technology . “QPUs promise to unlock new insights as they are very different from the hardware that we are used to. So having both GPUs and QPUs available within OCI would provide an all-in-one platform, simplify the operation of novel hardware, and help us move at speed from concept to execution by allowing our researchers to focus on innovation. It could herald in an exciting new phase for our work.” “As quantum computing moves closer to enterprise adoption, simplifying how organizations access and integrate quantum resources has become just as important as advancing the hardware itself,” said Heather West, PhD, Global Quantum Research Lead at IDC . “Deploying quantum systems within private cloud environments enables organizations to integrate quantum computing into existing AI and HPC workflows through familiar cloud infrastructure and development tools, reducing barriers to adoption and making hybrid quantum-classical computing a practical part of enterprise IT.” Contact Info Carolin Bachmann Oracle carolin.bachmann@oracle.com +1.415.622.8466 Aaron Sorenson Quantinuum aaron.sorenson@quantinuum.com About Quantinuum Quantinuum is a leading quantum computing company offering a full-stack platform designed to make quantum computing deployable in real-world environments. The company has commercially deployed multiple generations of trapped-ion based quantum systems built on the well-established QCCD architecture, which it has implemented with novel designs and capabilities to achieve the industry’s highest accuracy levels based on average two-qubit gate fidelity.3 Quantinuum has active engagements with market leaders across pharmaceuticals, material science, financial services, and government and industrial markets, as well as academic and research institutions globally. The company has a global workforce of approximately 700 employees, including top scientists and researchers. Over 70% of its technology team holds PhDs or Master’s degrees. Quantinuum’s headquarters is in Broomfield, Colorado, with additional facilities across the United States, United Kingdom, Germany, Japan, Qatar, and Singapore. For more information, please visit www.quantinuum.com . About Oracle Oracle offers integrated suites of applications plus secure, autonomous infrastructure in the Oracle Cloud. For more information about Oracle (NYSE: ORCL), please visit us at www.oracle.com . Trademarks Oracle, Java, MySQL, and NetSuite are registered trademarks of Oracle Corporation. NetSuite was the first cloud company—ushering in the new era of cloud computing.
